newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-PRESSURE MOUNTS ON BRITISH MANAGERS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PRESSURE MOUNTS ON BRITISH MANAGERS.

text.p: They were busy removing Kevin Keegan's name-plate from his parking space at St James' Park on Thursday less than 24 hours after his shock resignation as manager of Newcastle United.

In its place the club should erect a list of names designed to make Keegan's successor pause for a moment. Kenny Dalglish, Brian Clough, Graeme Souness, Bobby Robson, Graham Taylor, Steve Coppell....all of them well-known football men crushed at various times by the cares of management.

The exact reasons for Keegan's dramatic exit are still under debate but what is not in dispute is the increasing pressure on British soccer managers. If Newcastle fans were shocked by the news -- "Losing Kev feels worse than if the Queen died" -- many in the game were less surprised.

"There is too much pressure on people like Kevin," said Tottenham manager Gerry Francis. "I've been a manager for 11 years and I can honestly say there has never been as much to deal with as there is now."
Former Leeds manager Howard Wilkinson, installed this week as the Football Association's technical director, was equally sympathetic.

"The last time I saw him on television I thought he looked extremely ill. Compared with the day nearly five years ago when he became manager of Newcastle United, he appeared to have aged by at least 15 years. It came as no surprise to me yesterday when he resigned.
"Managers have always been under pressure to succeed but what is different today is the intensity of outside influences over which you have no control."

Keegan's departure swiftly demonstrated the point, raising almost as many financial questions as footballing ones with Newcastle poised to join the London Stock Exchange as well as aiming high on the pitch.

"There are now heightened expectations at all the top clubs," said John Williams, the country's leading soccer researcher. "Both fans and directors want accelerated success and that puts almost unbearable pressures on managers."

Few managers know what it feels like to spend 60 million pounds on players and still not win the league title, but all are experts on insecurity. Alex Ferguson has spent 10 years in charge of Manchester United, but the number of current managers who have remained at the same English club for a decade can be counted on the fingers of one hand.

Dalglish claimed he resigned from Liverpool in February 1991 because he felt his "head was going to explode", while Clough's 18-year reign at Nottingham Forest ended sadly amid tales of heavy drinking and Souness underwent a triple heart bypass operation while manager of Liverpool.

Robson and Taylor both aged visibly during their time in charge of England and younger men, like Coppell who lasted just 33 days as manager of Manchester City this season, have found themselves equally worn down by the weight of responsibility. Individual circumstances may differ but managers everywhere must be wondering if legendary former Liverpool manager Bill Shankly -- "Football's not a matter of life or death, it's more important than that" -- was accurately predicting how British soccer would develop in the late 1990s.
Restoring a sense of perspective will be Keegan's next challenge.
